proposed.text: Cellulose nitrate film fires cannot be extinguished by smothering (CO₂ or inert gas systems). What fundamental chemical property of cellulose nitrate makes conventional gas-based suppression ineffective?

options.text: Self-oxidizing — the film contains its own chemically bound oxygen and continues burning without external air supply
High surface-area-to-mass ratio — the film burns too quickly for smothering agents to take effect before combustion completes
Thermoplastic behavior — the film melts and flows, spreading fire even after surface oxygen is depleted by suppression
Catalytic decomposition — heat from suppression agents accelerates rather than suppresses combustion through exothermic reaction

proposed.rationale: Original question was already source-correct and substantive; the prior edit (source-audited-article-batch-048) was degenerate, with 1-character garbage in 3 of 4 option text fields and a nonsensical rationale. Restored the original verbatim. Original source rationale: Cellulose nitrate contains oxygen chemically bound within the nitrate ester groups of its polymer chain. This means it burns vigorously even in an oxygen-depleted atmosphere and cannot be extinguished by CO₂, Halon, or any smothering agent. Water or water solutions are the specified first aid agents because they absorb heat and reduce spread rate — the only effective approach against a self-oxidizing fire. The 1929 Cleveland Clinic disaster (123 deaths from toxic gas inhalation) was the historical catalyst for international film storage standards.
proposed.code_citation: PD 1096, Rule XII, Sec. 1212 / RA 9514 (Fire Code)
